_note: Narration for the OpenRiC five-minute demonstration. Ids match the marks in record.js exactly; a mark without an entry fails the build, which is the behaviour we want. Written as normal prose - pronunciation rules (RiC as Rick, RiC-O as Rick Oh, glTF, BM-125320) live in speak.py, not here, so this stays readable for whoever edits it next. Reflects the state of openric.org, viewer.openric.org and ric.theahg.co.za on 28 September 2026.

scenes.text: This is a model funeral boat from ancient Egypt. About four and a half thousand years old, British Museum number BM-125320. A catalogue record can tell you it exists, who holds it, and what it looks like. It cannot easily tell you that it was made in Thebes, moved to London, is governed today by a specific Egyptian statute, and now also exists as a downloadable three-D file. And it certainly cannot tell you that those four facts are connected to each other, rather than just to the record.

Here is the record on its own. A title, an identifier, a holder, a description. Useful, and roughly what any catalogue would give you. But look at the holder. It is not the text, The British Museum. It is a link, to the British Museum as a thing in its own right. Everything that follows comes from that one difference.

Now the same record, drawn with everything connected to it. Twenty-three things, twenty-two connections, in about two seconds. Places, the repository holding it, four separate activities, two pieces of legislation, and two digital files. None of this is a search result. Every line here is a stated, typed relationship that a machine can follow without guessing. The legend names them in plain language, and the trail along the top is how you find your way back.

Four activities sit in this graph, and together they are a life story. The boat being made, in Egypt. The archival creation event. A transfer into the collection that holds it now. And, in our own lifetime, a photogrammetry digitisation. This is the part traditional description handles worst. In an ordinary record, custody history is a paragraph of prose - readable by a person, invisible to everything else. Here, each step is an entity with its own date and place. And the digitisation is exactly the same kind of thing as the original production. Neither is privileged.

Two of these are laws. The Egyptian Antiquities Protection Law, number 117 of 1983, and a Giza protection ordinance. That is a genuinely hard thing to express anywhere else. The statute is not a property of the record, and not a note on it. It is a separate thing, with its own identity, which happens to govern this material and could govern thousands of other items too. Model it once, link it many times, and a question like, which of our holdings are affected by Law 117, becomes a query instead of a research project. And here is the three-D file. The record and its digital copy are distinct entities, which is how an archive holds six versions of a file without pretending it has six records.

One request, no key, no account, and the whole thing comes back as R D F, with every relationship intact. This is the part that matters if you are deciding whether to adopt anything. The graph you just walked is not locked inside that viewer. The viewer is an ordinary client, reading an open contract. Point a different conformant client at the same server and you get the same graph. Move your data to a different implementation and the relationships survive, because they are in the data rather than in somebody's schema.

One last thing, before you go looking. This is a working archive, not a showcase, and it has the rough edges you would expect. You will find a repository still labelled UPDATED from somebody's test edit, a duplicated Egypt, and three entities typed as activities that are plainly a place, an organisation and a family. We leave them visible on purpose. A demonstration built on hand-groomed data proves nothing about whether the model survives contact with real holdings.
OpenRiC is an open specification for publishing and exchanging Records in Contexts data. The contract, the reference implementation and the conformance tooling are all at openric dot org.
